1.pericope_label: The child ministering, the word of the Lord scarce, and the lamp not yet gone out

schools.summary: Remark how little the writer says about the childhood of a man second only to Moses, and read the brevity as evidence that the boy was kept from the party of Eli's sons; and take the opening verses as a single period whose circumstantial clauses light up the situation, so that the dimness of Eli's eyes is told not for its own sake but to explain why a boy hearing his name in the night would suppose the blind old man was calling him.

Take precious to mean scarce, since rare things are prized and common ones despised, and infer from the remark that the writer himself lived when prophecy was frequent; explain that there was then no accredited public prophet to be resorted to in emergency, while allowing that God might still reveal himself privately; note that this is premised to explain why Samuel did not understand the first call; and place the scene before sunrise, when the lamps were put out.

Make the child a rebuke to Eli's sons, whose wickedness was aggravated by being shamed by a boy, and draw the lesson that faithfulness in a little led to trust with much more, so that the young should be humble and diligent, since those are fittest to rule who have learnt to obey.

Fill out the boy's duties from tradition — the doors, the lamps, the singing — and his age from Josephus; note that some lamps went out by morning while the western one never did; and report the reading that makes the lamp the lamp of prophecy, not yet extinct in Eli when it rose in Samuel, as one sun sets only after another has arisen.

debates: What the child's ministry consisted of, and how old he was.
Whether precious means valued or merely scarce, and what the remark reveals about when the book was written.
Why the dimness of Eli's eyes and the burning of the lamp are mentioned at all.
Whether the lamp is the candlestick in the sanctuary or a figure for the gift of prophecy.
outliers: Ellicott alone comments on the disproportion between the man's importance and the brevity of the record of his childhood.
Clarke alone turns the scarcity of prophecy into evidence about the age in which the historian lived.
Keil alone treats the whole opening as one grammatical period and the intervening details as circumstantial.
Wesley alone explains that the notice is placed here to account for the boy's failure to recognise the voice.
Gill alone reports the figure of one sun rising before another sets, applied to Moses and Joshua as well as to Eli and Samuel.

4.pericope_label: The Lord calls Samuel three times, and Eli perceives who is calling

schools.summary: Place the voice in the most holy place between the cherubim, and supply the boy's motive for running, that he thought the old man needed help and hurried the more out of affection for his age; deny that he was ignorant of God, and locate his want, after Maimonides, in never having heard that God spoke to men in a familiar voice, so that he could not tell that voice from Eli's; and offer three accounts of the Lord standing, preferring the one that makes it a voice sounding nearer.

Suppose the voice came from the holy place near which both were lying; distinguish knowing and worshipping the God of Israel from knowing him as one who gives special revelations, and argue that the boy's ignorance served God's purpose, since his simplicity assured Eli the call was genuine; identify the words Eli taught him as the usual prophetic form; and explain the Lord standing as a voice heard approaching until its tone ceased to change.

Remark how naturally the story is told, the supernatural interwoven with the common life of the sanctuary until the reader forgets its strangeness, and reconstruct the unrecorded conversation by which Eli worked out that the voice came from the direction of the ark; and take the words that the Lord came and stood as proving the revelation objectively real and not a dream.

debates: Where the voice came from, and how near it was.
What Samuel lacked that kept him from recognising it, given that he already knew and served God.
How Eli arrived at the conclusion that the Lord was calling the child.
Whether the Lord standing describes a real presence or the boy's impression of an approaching voice.
outliers: Keil alone uses the words about standing to argue that the revelation was objectively real rather than a dream.
Clarke alone explains the standing acoustically, as a voice that stopped seeming to approach.
Ellicott alone invents the dialogue between the old priest and the boy that the narrative leaves out.
Wesley alone makes the boy's ignorance evidence for Eli of the truth of the call.
Gill alone reports the opinion that a corporeal form was seen, and sets it aside for a nearer voice.

11.pericope_label: The message against the house of Eli: the tingling ears and the oath that no sacrifice can purge

schools.summary: Note what the message is not — no telling of the boy's own future, since God came to employ him rather than gratify curiosity — and account for its brevity by the memory of a child, which must not be overcharged even with divine things; observe that threatenings disregarded come the surer and fall the heavier, and that the errand might serve Samuel later, when his own sons proved less good than they should have been.

Identify the coming calamity as the capture of the ark, unparalleled in the annals of the nation because it seemed to say God had forsaken them, and note that the singular phrase about tingling ears recurs only of the destruction of Jerusalem; settle the Hebrew, that judging a crime means punishing it and that for ever means the punishment is never lifted; measure Eli's sin by the unbelief his sons' example spread through the people; and find in the oath a limit to the efficacy of sacrifice, past which Eli must have looked to another deliverance.

Argue from the boy's age that he saw nothing and only heard; read the tingling as an aftersound that keeps resounding once heard; divide over the clause about beginning and ending, one making it exclude delay and the other allowing twenty or thirty years of space for repentance before an execution that will not stop; judge Eli guilty of a cold reproof where punishment was owed, and lay down that those who could restrain sin and do not share the guilt; and restrict the unpurgeable iniquity to temporal death.
Hold that the earlier prophecy by the man of God preceded this message, against the sense of some, and that the oath either had been sworn before or is sworn now to confirm the threat.

debates: Why the message says nothing about Samuel himself, and why it is so short.
What calamity is meant by the words about tingling ears.
Whether the words about beginning and making an end exclude all delay or only any reprieve once begun.
How far the declaration that no sacrifice can purge the iniquity extends.
outliers: Henry alone explains the brevity of the revelation by the memory of the child who had to carry it.
Clarke alone argues from Samuel's youth that nothing was seen, only heard.
Clarke and Wesley draw opposite conclusions from the same clause about beginning and ending.
Ellicott alone reads Eli's later resignation as evidence that he looked beyond the sacrifices to another victim.
Wesley alone turns Eli's failure into a general rule about the guilt of those who could restrain sin and do not.

15.pericope_label: Samuel fears to tell, Eli adjures him, and the old man submits

schools.summary: Observe that the text says Samuel lay till morning and not that he slept, since so strange an honour and so dreadful a message would keep a child waking; explain Eli's impatience by his having slighted the man of God who came before and questioned his authority; and draw the rule that the whole counsel of God is to be declared and nothing concealed, whether it please men or not.

Take the opening of doors as evidence that the tabernacle at Shiloh had been enclosed in permanent buildings; quote the prophet's cross of having unwelcome truth to tell those he loves; hold that Eli's reply proves him, for all his weakness and indulgence towards his sons, thoroughly devoted to the Lord in his heart, while judging that reformation had become impossible and he was by then a puppet of his sons; and credit Samuel with the courage to deliver a solemn word against a man he loved.

Note that God had given no command to deliver the message, so the boy kept silence until adjured, from reverence and from fear of distressing the old man — and lest haste be taken for arrogance or secret satisfaction in his calamity; read the adjuration as an imprecation of the same curses and greater; find in the answer godly submission and a deep sense of unworthiness, while cautioning that the sentence reached only to temporal death; and derive the word whit from the Anglo-Saxon.

debates: Whether Samuel slept that night, and what the wording implies.
What the mention of doors proves about the sanctuary at Shiloh.
Why Samuel kept silence until he was adjured.
What Eli's submission shows about him, and how far the sentence against him reached.
outliers: Gill alone rests an inference on the text saying that Samuel lay rather than that he slept.
Clarke alone points out that Samuel had received no command to deliver the message.
Wesley alone suggests the boy feared being thought to take satisfaction in the calamity he announced.
Ellicott reproduces Keil's verdict on Eli in nearly identical words, without acknowledgment.
Clarke alone enters a caution that the judgment on Eli reached no further than temporal death.

19.pericope_label: Samuel grows, none of his words falls to the ground, and all Israel knows him

schools.summary: Hear each brief notice about the boy as a contrast with somebody else, here with Eli, since the Lord was with both but only the young prophet let no word fall; collect the idiom of a word not falling from three other passages; render the word for established as found trustworthy and refer it to the verse calling Moses faithful in all God's house; and observe that the people were thereby prepared to acknowledge a God-sent chieftain, forming religiously a unit in spite of their disruption.

Take the growth of grace, wisdom and reputation together with that of stature; gloss the two towns as the northern and southern limits of the land; and place the renewed appearing at Shiloh immediately before the battle with the Philistines that follows.

Trace all increase in wisdom and grace to the presence of God, which is all in all to growth; suppose early instances of fulfilled prediction that satisfied the people about his mission; and take the renewal of the visions as showing that God repeats his visits to those who receive them aright.

Find in the words about falling a metaphor from precious liquors, useless once spilt; render the word for established as faithful; note that the last verse says God added to appear, meaning he continued to reveal himself; and close the chapter with an argument about religious education — that Eli neither taught nor restrained his children, that neglect joined to want of affectionate restraint is the ruin of millions, and that the parents who plead they cannot give their children grace are making God the author of their children's viciousness.

debates: In what senses Samuel grew, and to what his growth is owing.
Whether the brief notices of his progress are told for their own sake or as a contrast with Eli and his house.
Whether the word rendered established means confirmed in office or found faithful.
What responsibility parents bear for the character of their children.
outliers: Ellicott alone reads each notice of Samuel's progress as deliberately set against another life.
Wesley alone explains the words about falling by the image of spilt liquor.
Keil alone links the word for established to the verse in which Moses is called faithful.
Ellicott alone quotes the judgment that a divided people were nevertheless religiously one.
Clarke alone leaves the narrative for a sustained argument on education, and answers the plea that parents cannot give their children grace by charging it with making God the author of their vice.
